newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia leak reinforces "Big Brother" image.
newsitem.headline: Australia leak reinforces "Big Brother" image.

text.p: The leaking of a secret Australian report personally critical of South Pacific politicians will severely damage Australia's reputation among the tiny island nations and undermine its diplomatic goals.
The report has reinforced the belief that Australia is the "Big Brother" of the region with an arrogant, condescending and patronising attitude towards its smaller island neighbours.
Adding salt to the diplomatic wound is the region's colonial legacy -- Australia governed Papua New Guinea until 1975 and all the other South Pacific nations were once European colonies.
South Pacific diplomacy is a fragile affair where traditional courtesies are just as important as tough, back-room negotiations and where "the Pacific way" -- consensus -- rules.
Robust Western-style politics, where public attacks are a common weapon, sits uneasy in this region where clan or personal loyalties are often more powerful than party politics.
"We have our forum, we have our own ways of talking...for that report to be made the way it was, I believe, is a show of disrespect," said Fiji Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka.
In fact, Rabuka, who led a military coup in 1987, was once forced to drop to his knees and publicly apologise to his late paramount chief, then president Ratu Sir Penaia Ganilau.

In 1991 Fiji's newspapers ran front page photographs of Rabuka in front of Ganilau, presenting his chief with a "tabua" or sperm whale's tooth -- a "mata ni gasau" or traditional Fijian apology. Ganilau also ordered Rabuka to apologise to the then prime minister Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara.

Rabuka's offence? He was disrespectful. As head of Fiji's military, and more importantly as a commoner, he said the country's interim government headed by a chief should resign because it had lost credibility over its handling of a sugar cane farmers dispute.

This week a Tongan journalist was jailed and charged with sedition for publishing a letter questioning the policy of King Taufa'ahau Tupou IV's government. Last October, a Tongan editor was jailed for an article disrespectful to parliament.

Former Australian prime minister Paul Keating, renowned for being unpunctual, caused a diplomatic incident in 1992 when he arrived 10 minutes late for a South Pacific Forum meeting in the Solomon Islands.
In a region where punctuality sways with the palm trees it is fine to be late, but not to an official function. Like Japan, "face" is all-important in these tiny island nations.
To describe island politicians as corrupt drunks who have contributed to economic mayhem is not surprising in a secret document. Many governments and intelligence bodies compile such personal files.
But to allow such disparaging comments to become public, even by accidentally leaving the document on a coffee table for a journalist to pick up, is unforgivable in the South Pacific.

"I can assure you that this will take a very long time to be forgiven, if at all, right around the region," said Gareth Evans, Keating's long-serving foreign minister who has seen the South Pacific's wrath at first hand.
Ironically, the contents of the briefing paper are not startling revelations for the people of the South Pacific.
The economic woes of the South Pacific are well documented.

The Asian Development Bank has regularly issued pessimistic forecasts for island economies, warning that budget deficits pose a threat to economic stability. In May 1996, the bank said at least half the islands faced some form of economic crisis.

The islands have economies marked by low growth, bloated public sectors, weak private sectors and foreign aid accounting for up to 70 percent of gross domestic product. The Cook Islands is near bankruptcy after running up public debt of US$120 million in 1996 following a failed hotel development.
Corruption is also a widespread problem across the Pacific.

"We will fight corruption, but not destroy our own people," vowed Papua New Guinea's newly-elected prime minister Bill Skate on Tuesday. Corruption and economic management will also be major issues in the August election in the Solomon Islands.
As for the drinking habits of ministers, hard drinking is rooted in traditional South Pacific ceremonies and the habits of turn-of-the-century explorers and whalers.
Australia is the region's major aid donor contributing A$124.7 million annually and has often issued stern warnings to the islands about their economic management.
In 1994 it said environmental degradation in the South Pacific was fuelled by bribery and corruption and the region was doomed unless governments adopted sustainable economic policies.
But the personal criticism in the secret report has crossed the diplomatic 'line in the sand' in the South Pacific and will not quickly be washed away.
